claim: To cut new topology across an existing face without creating a T-junction ngon on that face's unselected neighbors, select the target vertices and press J (Connect Vertex Path) rather than subdividing/bisecting the shared boundary edge. J splits the existing face itself along the shortest path between the selected vertices -- it does not insert a new vertex into a boundary edge shared with a face outside the selection, which is what creates a T-junction on the neighbor.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation (2026-08-15, Mesh Modeling chapter pass, 29:22-58:16): at 30:15-30:45, pressing F creates a floating edge overlaying a face without splitting it, while J splits the face itself along the shortest vertex-to-vertex path, explicitly framed as avoiding hidden ngons/T-junctions and redirecting edge flow without overlapping geometry.
rejected_alternative: subdivide_selection/bisect_selection on a single face or small selected subset, which cuts the shared boundary edge and leaves an unselected neighbor face with a mid-edge vertex it doesn't know about -- the repeatedly-confirmed T-junction ngon bug from the padlock shackle-hole attempts (three separate rejected attempts, 2026-08-14/15).
reason: This project's typed mesh_ops.py has no connect_vertex_path-equivalent operation yet -- only subdivide_selection and bisect_selection exist for adding topology, both of which hit the T-junction bug whenever the cut touches a boundary edge shared with unselected geometry. This is the first concrete, sourced fix candidate for that bug rather than just a documented limitation to work around.

claim: Bridge Edge Loops (Ctrl+E) can punch a clean through-hole between two opposing, coplanar, matching-vertex-count face selections in a single operation, rather than requiring a separate subdivide/bisect step to first create the hole boundary.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 43:21-43:47, selecting two opposing parallel faces with matching vertex counts and running Bridge Edge Loops instantly creates a through-hole, framed as avoiding destructive boolean-cutter artifacts.
rejected_alternative: Cutting a hole boundary into an existing face via subdivide/bisect first, then deleting the interior and bridging or filling -- the multi-step approach that hit the T-junction bug on the padlock shackle-hole attempts.
reason: This is a second, independent alternative to the T-junction-prone subdivide/bisect approach for creating holes -- if two matching loops can be positioned directly (e.g. via two separate insets at the same size on opposite faces), bridging between them sidesteps the boundary-edge-sharing problem entirely.

claim: Loop Tools' Circle operator takes a selected rectangular/quad face patch and reshapes it into a perfect circular loop in place, without manual vertex-by-vertex positioning -- the stated standard technique for embedding clean circular holes/bosses into flat or curved topology.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 56:32-57:41, the Loop Tools add-on's Circle function converts a selected face patch into a circular loop, and Flatten planarizes skewed faces; framed as "the gold standard for embedding clean, circular holes into flat and curved topology."
rejected_alternative: Manually computing circle points (as done for the padlock shackle's semicircular arc via explicit cosine/sine parametrization) or using a boolean cylinder cutter for circular holes.
reason: A third alternative for circular-hole geometry (alongside the connect-vertex-path fix and the bridge-based hole technique above) -- relevant to any future circular hole/boss requirement (bolt holes, vents, circular bosses) without hand-computing an arc.

claim: Grid Fill (Ctrl+F -> Grid Fill) fills an open loop with an even vertex count with a complete all-quad grid (with adjustable Span/Offset), replacing what would otherwise be a single large ngon or a manual triangle fan.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 37:24-37:55, Grid Fill converts an even-count open boundary loop into a subdividable all-quad surface, contrasted directly with messy triangle fans or large ngons on cylinder caps/rounded surfaces.
rejected_alternative: fill_selection producing a single ngon cap, or a manual triangle fan, both of which pass automated manifold/ngon checks poorly or produce non-radial quad flow (see mesh-validity-vs-mesh-quality memory: automated checks alone don't catch bad topology).
reason: Directly applicable to capping any cylindrical or rounded boundary loop in this project (teapot/mug lids, padlock shackle-hole rims) with real quad topology instead of an ngon.

claim: Select All by Trait -> Non-Manifold selects every open boundary edge on a mesh at once; combined with Fill (F), Triangulate (Ctrl+T), and Tris to Quads (Alt+J), this closes every open hole on a complex asset in one batch pass rather than hunting for holes individually.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 39:36-40:26, Select All by Trait -> Non-Manifold selects boundary loops across the whole mesh, then Fill + Triangulate + Tris-to-Quads seals them in one pass; framed as fixing broken scanned/boolean geometry in batches.
rejected_alternative: Manually locating and filling each open boundary loop one at a time.
reason: A useful health-check/repair pass to run after any operation suspected of leaving unintended open boundaries (e.g. after a rejected/partially-reverted decision transaction), complementing the existing get_full_state mesh_health.non_manifold_edges check with an actual fix action, not just a diagnostic count.

claim: Offset Edge Slide (Ctrl+Shift+R) spawns two new parallel, symmetric holding/support loops straddling an existing edge loop in one operation (with Even/Flip parity controls), rather than requiring two separate single loop cuts placed by hand.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 46:56-48:00, Ctrl+Shift+R creates two parallel holding loops around an existing edge loop simultaneously, described as the primary method for placing tight support loops that control Subdivision Surface falloff near mechanical seams.
rejected_alternative: Placing two separate loop cuts by hand on either side of a seam edge and manually adjusting each one's offset to keep them symmetric.
reason: Directly relevant to this project's standing bevel-weight/SubD policy: genuinely sharp edges need either a real Bevel or tight holding loops to stay crisp under Subdivision Surface -- this is the loop-cut-based alternative to a geometric Bevel for that same goal.

claim: The built-in Bool Tool add-on's Auto Boolean shortcuts (Difference/Union/Intersect/Slice) perform a full destructive boolean and immediately apply+clean the modifier in one step, versus manually adding a Boolean modifier, setting its operand object, applying it, and deleting the leftover cutter object.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 54:50-56:31, the Bool Tool add-on executes fast destructive Auto Booleans or non-destructive Brush Booleans with automated wireframe cutter management, described as drastically accelerating hard-surface boolean workflows.
rejected_alternative: The project's current manual boolean sequence (add_modifier BOOLEAN, set_modifier_parameter object/operation, apply, then delete the cutter object) -- functionally equivalent but more typed-op calls per boolean cut.
reason: A workflow-efficiency note, not a capability gap: this project's typed add_modifier/set_modifier_parameter path already reaches the same destructive-boolean result; Bool Tool is a Blender-side convenience layer worth knowing about but not something the typed op surface needs to replicate.

claim: Merge by Distance (M -> By Distance) removes duplicate/doubled coincident vertices left over from cancelled extrudes or manual bridging; Collapse (M -> Collapse) instead merges an entire connected vertex selection down to one point.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 31:57-32:42, M -> By Distance removes doubled vertices from cancelled duplicate/extrude/bridge operations, and Collapse merges a connected cluster into a single point; framed as preventing subdivision artifacts, bevel pinching, and boolean failures.
rejected_alternative: Leaving near-duplicate vertices in place after an interrupted or corrected operation, trusting later operations to tolerate them.
reason: This project's mesh_ops.py already exposes merge_by_distance as a typed op -- this confirms it against an independent source and clarifies the specific failure mode it targets (cancelled extrude/bridge doubles), useful context for when to reach for it proactively rather than only when a health check flags a problem.
